system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated by chronic marginal (gastrojejunal) ulcer and post-bypass hypoglycemia requiring continuous gastrostomy tube feeds was admitted for acute-on-chronic left upper quadrant abdominal pain localized near the G-tube site and worsened with tube feed infusion. Evaluation showed stable vital signs, reassuring abdominal exam without peritonitis, normal laboratory studies, and a chest radiograph without free air; there was no evidence of tube-site infection. Bariatric surgery recommended no additional imaging or surgical intervention, and the pain was felt most consistent with her known marginal ulcer and/or local tube-site irritation. She received IV analgesia initially, continued ulcer therapy with lansoprazole and sucralfate via tube, and tube feeds were restarted without difficulty to prevent hypoglycemia (supported with dextrose-containing IV fluids while feeds were off). Symptoms improved with pain control, and she was discharged home ambulatory with liquid oxycodone as needed and instructions to follow up with pain management and keep her planned end-of-month EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the doctor on the medicine team. I hear you came in with severe pain around your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same deep pain right under the tube and in the middle of my upper belly, but it got way worse after they changed the tube in clinic yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Is it mostly at the skin, or does it feel deeper—like inside the abdomen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Deeper. The skin is sore, but the worst is deep. I feel nauseated too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, diarrhea, fevers, chills, or sweats?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just nausea. No fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How have your tube feeds been going—any trouble running them, or does the pain change when feeds are going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need them constantly or my sugar drops. The pain is just there all the time, but it’s worse since the exchange.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I also see you were recently discharged for similar pain and were supposed to use liquid oxycodone. Were you able to get it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I couldn’t find the liquid anywhere, so I’ve been crushing pills and putting them through the tube. I don’t think it’s working right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense—crushing can change how it absorbs and can irritate the tube. In the ED your labs looked okay, and the chest X-ray didn’t show free air, which is reassuring. Surgery saw some irritation at the site and recommended admission for pain control and to make sure there’s no deeper problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s in the wrong place again. That happened before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, that’s a very reasonable concern. The next step is a CT scan of your abdomen with contrast to confirm the tube position and look for bleeding, a collection, or an abscess around the tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the CT hurt? And can I keep my feeds running? I don’t want my sugar to crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT itself shouldn’t be painful—just lying still. We may pause feeds briefly for the scan, but we’ll monitor your fingerstick glucose and keep you safe. We’ll check sugars every six hours while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain is really bad right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll treat your pain. We’ll use liquid oxycodone here so it’s easier on the tube, and we’ll also use acetaminophen as a baseline. We’ll avoid NSAIDs because of your marginal ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this from the ulcer again? It feels like it’s right at the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be a mix. The tenderness is at the tube site, but you also describe epigastric pain, and you have a known chronic marginal ulcer. Frequent manipulation of the tube can also irritate the tract and the abdominal wall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m going to examine the site now. I see a small amount of whitish drainage and some focal redness, but no spreading redness or warmth. Your vitals are stable and your white blood cell count is normal, which makes a serious infection less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So do I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, without fever, spreading redness, or a high white count, we’re not seeing signs of a deeper infection. We’ll keep the area clean and continue the topical ointment you use, and the CT will help us confirm there’s no abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is still there. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—we can give medication for nausea as needed. Also, we’ll continue your ulcer medicines—lansoprazole and sucralfate—through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: surgery reviewed you again this morning. We’re proceeding with the CT abdomen with contrast today to check tube position and look for any complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the CT is normal, what then? I can’t keep coming back like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s normal, we focus on symptom control and preventing hypoglycemia, and we coordinate follow-up with your primary doctor and your surgeons. We also want to be careful with opioids—sometimes with chronic use, pain can actually become more sensitive, so we’ll aim for the lowest effective dose and a plan for outpatient management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They restarted my tube feeds, right? I feel shaky when they stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your continuous tube feeds are running. We’ll keep checking fingersticks and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT is back. The G-tube balloon is in the stomach where it should be. There are some inflammatory changes in the abdominal wall muscle where the tube goes in, but there’s no hematoma, no abscess, and no discrete fluid collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not misplaced and it’s not an abscess?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no misplacement and no abscess seen. That supports the idea that this is irritation/inflammation at the tract plus your chronic ulcer-related pain, rather than a dangerous complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can be severe even without a collection—especially when the abdominal wall is inflamed and when there’s chronic pain in the background. The recent tube exchange can flare things up. Our goal is to get you comfortable enough to go home safely while keeping your sugars stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oxycodone helps some, but I’m worried I’ll run out again or not find the liquid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prescribe tablets you can take by mouth as directed, and we’ll make sure you have a clear plan for refills through bariatric surgery and pain management rather than the emergency room. We’ll also add acetaminophen to reduce how much opioid you need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting or new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is still there but not as sharp as yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Your sugars have been stable on the continuous feeds. We’ll keep your ulcer medications going and continue to avoid NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little lightheaded when I stand up. Is that from the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from the pain meds, but your blood pressure has also been running low. I see you’re on atenolol at home. Did you take it recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took it like I always do. Sometimes my pressure is low and I skip it, but I didn’t this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think the atenolol is contributing to the low blood pressure, especially if you’re a bit dry from not feeling well. You’re not having chest pain or shortness of breath, and your heart rhythm looks like normal sinus rhythm. We’re going to stop the atenolol here and give you IV fluids to bring the pressure up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to just stop it? I thought you can’t stop those suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In your case, given the low pressures, it’s safer to hold it. We’ll monitor you closely. Also, beta blockers like atenolol can mask symptoms of low blood sugar, which is a concern for you since you’re at risk of hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pressure feels better after the fluids. Does that mean I shouldn’t take atenolol anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend not restarting it for now. We’ll document that clearly and ask you to follow up with your primary care doctor to reassess your blood pressure plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site still looks a little red. Should I be worried about MRSA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your history of MRSA is important, but right now we’re not seeing signs of a spreading infection—no fever, no worsening redness, and the CT didn’t show an abscess. Keep using the mupirocin as prescribed and watch for warning signs like increasing redness, warmth, pus, fever, or feeling ill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning your pain seems improved compared with admission. If you feel comfortable with the plan, we can discharge you today with medications and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home and the pain coming back. What do I do if it spikes again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the oxycodone as prescribed for breakthrough pain and acetaminophen as directed. Keep your ulcer medications—lansoprazole and sucralfate—consistent. Avoid NSAIDs. If you develop fever, vomiting that won’t stop, worsening redness around the tube, or severe worsening pain that feels different, you should seek urgent care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I still supposed to get that scope for the ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—there’s a plan for an EGD at the end of the month per prior notes. That’s important to reassess the marginal ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tube feeds—no changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes today. Continue your continuous tube feeds as you’ve been doing to prevent hypoglycemia, and keep checking your sugars as you normally do. We monitored fingersticks here and they stayed stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How much oxycodone are you sending me with? I don’t want to be stuck without it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re providing a two-week supply: oxycodone 10 mg, one tablet every 4 hours as needed, total 84 tablets. After that, ongoing prescriptions should come from bariatric surgery and/or pain management, not the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And just to confirm—no more atenolol at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—do not restart atenolol. Your blood pressures were low here, and it can also hide low blood sugar symptoms. Please follow up with your primary care doctor soon after discharge to review blood pressure management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’re stable, walking independently, and your pain is improved. You’ll go home on your home meds, continue tube feeds, continue lansoprazole and sucralfate, and use oxycodone and acetaminophen for pain. Follow up with your PCP and your surgeon. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, that covers it. I just hope it settles down. Thank you for explaining everything.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated by chronic marginal (gastrojejunal) ulcer and post-bypass hypoglycemia requiring continuous gastrostomy tube feeds was admitted for recurrent severe epigastric and deep G-tube–site pain that worsened after an outpatient G-tube exchange and difficulty obtaining liquid oxycodone. Initial evaluation showed stable vital signs, normal labs, and chest radiograph without free air. CT abdomen with contrast confirmed the G-tube balloon in the gastric fundus with inflammatory changes at the abdominal wall insertion site but no hematoma, abscess, or discrete collection. Pain improved with medical management including liquid oxycodone and acetaminophen while continuing lansoprazole and sucralfate and maintaining continuous tube feeds with glucose monitoring. During the stay she developed asymptomatic hypotension felt related to atenolol and relative hypovolemia; atenolol was stopped and fluids given with improvement. She was discharged home ambulatory with a two-week supply of oxycodone, instructions to avoid NSAIDs, continue tube feeds and ulcer therapy, and follow up with her PCP and surgical/pain teams.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the doctor on the medicine team. I hear you came in with severe pain around your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same deep pain right under the tube and in the middle of my upper belly, but it got way worse after they changed the tube in clinic yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Is it mostly at the skin, or does it feel deeper—like inside the abdomen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Deeper. The skin is sore, but the worst is deep. I feel nauseated too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, diarrhea, fevers, chills, or sweats?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just nausea. No fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How have your tube feeds been going—any trouble running them, or does the pain change when feeds are going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need them constantly or my sugar drops. The pain is just there all the time, but it’s worse since the exchange.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I also see you were recently discharged for similar pain and were supposed to use liquid oxycodone. Were you able to get it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I couldn’t find the liquid anywhere, so I’ve been crushing pills and putting them through the tube. I don’t think it’s working right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense—crushing can change how it absorbs and can irritate the tube. In the ED your labs looked okay, and the chest X-ray didn’t show free air, which is reassuring. Surgery saw some irritation at the site and recommended admission for pain control and to make sure there’s no deeper problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s in the wrong place again. That happened before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, that’s a very reasonable concern. The next step is a CT scan of your abdomen with contrast to confirm the tube position and look for bleeding, a collection, or an abscess around the tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the CT hurt? And can I keep my feeds running? I don’t want my sugar to crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT itself shouldn’t be painful—just lying still. We may pause feeds briefly for the scan, but we’ll monitor your fingerstick glucose and keep you safe. We’ll check sugars every six hours while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain is really bad right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll treat your pain. We’ll use liquid oxycodone here so it’s easier on the tube, and we’ll also use acetaminophen as a baseline. We’ll avoid NSAIDs because of your marginal ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this from the ulcer again? It feels like it’s right at the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be a mix. The tenderness is at the tube site, but you also describe epigastric pain, and you have a known chronic marginal ulcer. Frequent manipulation of the tube can also irritate the tract and the abdominal wall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m going to examine the site now. I see a small amount of whitish drainage and some focal redness, but no spreading redness or warmth. Your vitals are stable and your white blood cell count is normal, which makes a serious infection less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So do I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, without fever, spreading redness, or a high white count, we’re not seeing signs of a deeper infection. We’ll keep the area clean and continue the topical ointment you use, and the CT will help us confirm there’s no abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is still there. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—we can give medication for nausea as needed. Also, we’ll continue your ulcer medicines—lansoprazole and sucralfate—through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: surgery reviewed you again this morning. We’re proceeding with the CT abdomen with contrast today to check tube position and look for any complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the CT is normal, what then? I can’t keep coming back like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s normal, we focus on symptom control and preventing hypoglycemia, and we coordinate follow-up with your primary doctor and your surgeons. We also want to be careful with opioids—sometimes with chronic use, pain can actually become more sensitive, so we’ll aim for the lowest effective dose and a plan for outpatient management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They restarted my tube feeds, right? I feel shaky when they stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your continuous tube feeds are running. We’ll keep checking fingersticks and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT is back. The G-tube balloon is in the stomach where it should be. There are some inflammatory changes in the abdominal wall muscle where the tube goes in, but there’s no hematoma, no abscess, and no discrete fluid collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not misplaced and it’s not an abscess?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no misplacement and no abscess seen. That supports the idea that this is irritation/inflammation at the tract plus your chronic ulcer-related pain, rather than a dangerous complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can be severe even without a collection—especially when the abdominal wall is inflamed and when there’s chronic pain in the background. The recent tube exchange can flare things up. Our goal is to get you comfortable enough to go home safely while keeping your sugars stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oxycodone helps some, but I’m worried I’ll run out again or not find the liquid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prescribe tablets you can take by mouth as directed, and we’ll make sure you have a clear plan for refills through bariatric surgery and pain management rather than the emergency room. We’ll also add acetaminophen to reduce how much opioid you need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting or new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is still there but not as sharp as yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Your sugars have been stable on the continuous feeds. We’ll keep your ulcer medications going and continue to avoid NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little lightheaded when I stand up. Is that from the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from the pain meds, but your blood pressure has also been running low. I see you’re on atenolol at home. Did you take it recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took it like I always do. Sometimes my pressure is low and I skip it, but I didn’t this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think the atenolol is contributing to the low blood pressure, especially if you’re a bit dry from not feeling well. You’re not having chest pain or shortness of breath, and your heart rhythm looks like normal sinus rhythm. We’re going to stop the atenolol here and give you IV fluids to bring the pressure up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to just stop it? I thought you can’t stop those suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In your case, given the low pressures, it’s safer to hold it. We’ll monitor you closely. Also, beta blockers like atenolol can mask symptoms of low blood sugar, which is a concern for you since you’re at risk of hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pressure feels better after the fluids. Does that mean I shouldn’t take atenolol anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend not restarting it for now. We’ll document that clearly and ask you to follow up with your primary care doctor to reassess your blood pressure plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site still looks a little red. Should I be worried about MRSA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your history of MRSA is important, but right now we’re not seeing signs of a spreading infection—no fever, no worsening redness, and the CT didn’t show an abscess. Keep using the mupirocin as prescribed and watch for warning signs like increasing redness, warmth, pus, fever, or feeling ill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning your pain seems improved compared with admission. If you feel comfortable with the plan, we can discharge you today with medications and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home and the pain coming back. What do I do if it spikes again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the oxycodone as prescribed for breakthrough pain and acetaminophen as directed. Keep your ulcer medications—lansoprazole and sucralfate—consistent. Avoid NSAIDs. If you develop fever, vomiting that won’t stop, worsening redness around the tube, or severe worsening pain that feels different, you should seek urgent care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I still supposed to get that scope for the ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—there’s a plan for an EGD at the end of the month per prior notes. That’s important to reassess the marginal ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tube feeds—no changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes today. Continue your continuous tube feeds as you’ve been doing to prevent hypoglycemia, and keep checking your sugars as you normally do. We monitored fingersticks here and they stayed stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How much oxycodone are you sending me with? I don’t want to be stuck without it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re providing a two-week supply: oxycodone 10 mg, one tablet every 4 hours as needed, total 84 tablets. After that, ongoing prescriptions should come from bariatric surgery and/or pain management, not the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And just to confirm—no more atenolol at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—do not restart atenolol. Your blood pressures were low here, and it can also hide low blood sugar symptoms. Please follow up with your primary care doctor soon after discharge to review blood pressure management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’re stable, walking independently, and your pain is improved. You’ll go home on your home meds, continue tube feeds, continue lansoprazole and sucralfate, and use oxycodone and acetaminophen for pain. Follow up with your PCP and your surgeon. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, that covers it. I just hope it settles down. Thank you for explaining everything.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated by chronic marginal (gastrojejunal) ulcer and post-bypass hypoglycemia requiring continuous gastrostomy tube feeds was admitted for recurrent severe epigastric and deep G-tube–site pain that worsened after an outpatient G-tube exchange and difficulty obtaining liquid oxycodone. Initial evaluation showed stable vital signs, normal labs, and chest radiograph without free air. CT abdomen with contrast confirmed the G-tube balloon in the gastric fundus with inflammatory changes at the abdominal wall insertion site but no hematoma, abscess, or discrete collection. Pain improved with medical management including liquid oxycodone and acetaminophen while continuing lansoprazole and sucralfate and maintaining continuous tube feeds with glucose monitoring. During the stay she developed asymptomatic hypotension felt related to atenolol and relative hypovolemia; atenolol was stopped and fluids given with improvement. She was discharged home ambulatory with a two-week supply of oxycodone, instructions to avoid NSAIDs, continue tube feeds and ulcer therapy, and follow up with her PCP and surgical/pain teams.
